{{Short description|Scottish-Jewish mathematician and philosopher (1889–1975)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2021}}

'''Hyman Levy''' {{Post-nominals|post-noms=[[Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh|FRSE]]}} (28 February 1889 – 27 February 1975)<ref name="DNB">{{cite dictionary |last=Stewart |first=John |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/31356 |url-access=subscription |title=Levy, Hyman (1889–1975) |dictionary=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |publisher=Oxford University Press |date=23 September 2004 |access-date=12 February 2023}}</ref>{{efn|''Who's Who'' records his birth date as 7 March 1889. See {{Who's Who | title=LEVY, Hyman | id = U156729 | type = was | volume = 2023 | edition = online}}}} was a Scottish-Jewish mathematician, philosopher, author, political activist, and fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]].<ref name=GfS>{{cite web |url=https://www.scottish-places.info/people/famousfirst836.html |title=Hyman Levy |website=[[Gazetteer for Scotland]] |access-date=10 February 2010}}</ref> For many years he taught mathematics at [[Imperial College London]], eventually retiring as [[Emeritus Professor]].

==Life==
Hyman Levy was born into an [[Orthodox Judaism|orthodox Jewish]] family in Scotland in 1889.<ref name=MacTutor/> He was the third oldest of eight children of Minna Cohen and Marcus Levy. His father was a picture-framer and occasional art dealer in [[Edinburgh]].<ref name=MacTutor>{{MacTutor|id=Levy_Hyman|title=Hyman Levy}}</ref> The family lived at 70 Bristo Street in Edinburgh's South Side.<ref>Edinburgh and Leith Post Office Directory 1890–91</ref>

Levy attended [[George Heriot's School]]<ref name=Times>Facsimile of the [https://web.archive.org/web/20120219232533/http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Obits/Levy_Hyman.html obituary, "Professor Hyman Levy"], published in ''[[The Times]]'', reproduced by [https://web.archive.org/web/20120219232537/http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/References/Levy_Hyman.html University of St Andrews]</ref> a short distance from his family home, and was named the school ''[[Dux]]'' in 1907.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.george-heriots.com/former-pupils/other-items-for-fps/school-captains-and-duxes |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191209121643/http://www.george-heriots.com/former-pupils/other-items-for-fps/school-captains-and-duxes |url-status=dead |archive-date=9 December 2019 |title=School Captains and Duxes George Heriot's School |website=www.george-heriots.com}}</ref> He studied mathematics at [[Edinburgh University]]. His leftist politics were evident early when he declined a chance for further study at [[Cambridge University]]—on account of what he considered its complicity in Britain's class system—and instead chose to pursue mathematical research at the [[University of Göttingen]] in Germany.<ref name="DNB"/><ref name=MacTutor/> At the outbreak of [[World War I]], Levy returned to Britain. In 1916 he joined the [[Royal Flying Corps]].<ref name=Biog_index /> It is unclear if he saw active service, but the experience inspired an interest in aerodynamics.

In 1916 he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]]. His proposers were [[Cargill Gilston Knott]], [[Edmund Taylor Whittaker]], [[James Robert Milne]] and [[George Carse|George Alexander Carse]].<ref name=Biog_index>{{cite book |title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002 |date=July 2006 |publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh |url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074135/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf |access-date=13 April 2017 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |url-status=dead |isbn=090219884X}}</ref>

In 1918 he married Marion Aitken Fraser, a devout [[Presbyterian]],<ref name=Times/> which led to a rupture with his family who disapproved of the interfaith marriage.<ref name=MacTutor/> The couple had a daughter and two sons.

Levy researched [[aeronautics]] at the [[National Physical Laboratory (United Kingdom)|National Physical Laboratory]] (NPL). He published papers and books on the subject, including ''Aeronautics in Theory and Experiment'' (1918), which was called "perhaps the earliest text covering, at advanced level, the whole theory of aeroplane design and operation."<ref>{{cite dictionary |last=Barnard |first=G. A. |title=Hyman Levy |dictionary=[[Dictionary of National Biography]], 1971–1980 |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1986 |pages=503–504 |editor-last1=Blake |editor-first1=Lord |editor-last2=Nicholls |editor-first2=C. S. |isbn=978-0198652083}}</ref> After leaving NPL, he became a professor of mathematics at the [[Royal College of Science]], [[Imperial College London]], where he later served as head of the mathematics department, and subsequently became dean of the Royal College itself.<ref name=MacTutor/>

Levy's main areas of mathematical specialization were in numerical methods, numerical solutions of [[differential equations]], finite difference equations and statistics.<ref name=MacTutor/> Among his important books were ''Numerical Studies in Differential Equations'' (1934), ''Elements of Probability'' (1936), and ''Finite Difference Equations'' (1959). He also made contributions to [[number theory]], including a 1963 paper comparing [[Lemoine's conjecture]] to [[Goldbach's weak conjecture]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Levy |first=H. |title=On Goldbach's Conjecture |journal=[[The Mathematical Gazette]] |volume=47 |date=1963 |page=274}}</ref><ref>{{MathWorld|title=Levy's Conjecture|urlname=LevysConjecture}} This ''[[MathWorld]]'' entry incorrectly refers to Lemoine's Conjecture as Levy's Conjecture.</ref>

Levy was in the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] from 1920 to 1931. He then joined the [[British Communist Party|Communist Party of Great Britain]] (CPGB), and was a loyal member for 25 years. In 1956 he travelled to the Soviet Union and was appalled by what he regarded as the mistreatment of Russian-Jewish writers, artists and intellectuals.<ref name=Stevenson>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Hyman Levy |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Communist Biographies |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211020042723/https://grahamstevenson.me.uk/2008/09/19/hyman-levy/ |url=https://grahamstevenson.me.uk/2008/09/19/hyman-levy/ |publisher=[[Graham Stevenson (trade union leader)|Graham Stevenson]] |archive-date=20 October 2021 |date=19 September 2008}}</ref> He published a scathing article on the subject in January 1957, and then followed that with a book, ''Jews and the National Question''. He was condemned by CPGB leadership for his "departure from Marxism",<ref name=Stevenson /> culminating in his expulsion from the Party in 1958.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Morgan |first1=Kevin |last2=Cohen |first2=Gidon |last3=Flinn |first3=Andrew |year=2007 |title=Communists and British Society, 1920-1991 |publisher=Rivers Oram Press |page=196 |isbn=978-1854891440}}</ref>

Hyman Levy died in [[Wimbledon, London]] on 27 February 1975,<ref name=Biog_index /> one day before his 86th birthday.

* ''The web of thought and action''. London: Watts (1934); {{OCLC|1899779}}.
* ''Aspects of Dialectical Materialism'', co-authored with [[Ralph Winston Fox]], [[John Macmurray]], [[R. Page Arnot]], [[J. D. Bernal]] and [[E. F. Carritt]]. London: Watts (1934); {{OCLC|5153156}}.
* ''Numerical Studies in Differential Equations'', co-authored with Edward Albert Baggott. London: Watts (1934); {{LCCN|34040900}}.
* ''Modern Engineering Theory & Practice'', co-authored with Bailey Levy; Odhams Press Ltd (1935); {{ASIN|B000R7AJPW}}.
* ''Elements of Probability'', co-authored with Leonard Roth. Oxford: The Clarendon Press (1936); {{LCCN|37010467}}.
* ''A Philosophy for a Modern Man''; Alfred A. Knopf (1938); {{ASIN|B0006DA3US}}.
* ''Modern Science – A Study of Physical Science in the World Today'', Hamish Hamilton (1939); {{ASIN|B00085G0RO}}.<ref>{{cite journal |author=MacDonald, J. K. Soc. |year=1940 |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=209–210 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1940-46-03/S0002-9904-1940-07166-6/S0002-9904-1940-07166-6.pdf |doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1940-07166-6 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* ''Science: Curse Or Blessing?'', London: Watts & Co. (1940); {{ASIN|B0026OCT8O}}.
* ''Elementary Mathematics'', London: Thomas Nelson & Sons (1942); {{ASIN|B0007DT7RC}}.
* ''Soviet Jews at war'', pamphlet, Russia Today Society (1943); {{ASIN|B00KBTLNDI}}.
